transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

Well, Doc, I guess what brings me in is I just keep forgetting things I really shouldn’t. Important stuff, you know? Like my heart follow-up appointments. I’ll completely miss them, or I'll forget to call the clinic back when they leave a message. Which reminds me, the receptionist at that clinic, she has the exact same voice as my sister-in-law. It’s uncanny. Every time she calls, I think it’s Martha calling to complain about her gutters again. I told Martha she needs to just bite the bullet and get those leaf guards installed, but she won't listen. 

Anyway, where was I? Oh, right, forgetting things. It’s not just the doctors. I do a lot of tinkering and repair jobs around the neighborhood since I retired, just to keep busy, you know? And I’ll show up to fix a cabinet or a pipe, and I completely forgot to bring the right tools. I’ll have a whole toolbox with me and not a single wrench I actually need for the job. It's just getting frustrating.
Have these forgetfulness problems been a change from how you used to be, or have you always been this forgetful?

Change? No, no, I wouldn't call it a change. It's pretty much the story of my life, honestly. Even way back as a boy in grade school, I was always that kid, you know? The one who just couldn’t stay in his seat to save his life. I was always blurting out answers before the teacher even finished the question, and getting notes sent home constantly for talking too much. 

Speaking of those notes, my third-grade teacher, Mrs. Higgins... she used to actually pin them to my jacket. With safety pins! Just right there on the lapel so I couldn't pretend I lost it on the walk home. Can you imagine a teacher doing that nowadays? The parents would throw an absolute fit, probably call the news stations! But back then, my mother would just unpin it, shake her head, and make me go peel potatoes for supper. We ate a lot of potatoes back then. Mashed, boiled, fried... my uncle grew them out on his farm and he'd send us these massive burlap sacks every fall. Have you ever tried to drag a fifty-pound sack of potatoes across a linoleum floor when you're eight years old? It builds character, I'll tell you that much. The dust gets everywhere, though. 

But, uh... anyway, what was the question? Oh, right, if this is new. No, Doc, I've pretty much always been this way.
